title: A Systematic Study of Security Enforcementat Android Inter-Component Boundaries An Empirical Evaluation of First-Party Interfacesand Platform Security Guardrails on Android 17

paper.title: A Systematic Study of Security Enforcement at Android Inter-Component Boundaries An Empirical Evaluation of First-Party Interfaces and Platform Security Guardrails on Android 17
paper.abstract: Abstract Android’s inter-process communication (IPC) mechanisms (Activities, Services, BroadcastReceivers, ContentProviders, and URI scheme handlers) form the primary interface between applications and between applications and the system. We present a systematic study of security enforcement comprising 120 evaluations (99 inter-component interface evaluations across five interface categories, 10 platform security-control evaluations, and 11 dedicated positive controls) in over 30 Google and AOSP packages on Android 17 (API 37). Using an expected-versus-observed framework under a zero-permission attacker model, we evaluate whether each boundary’s enforcement mechanism functions as designed. We find 97 enforcement gaps (80.8%) and 23 enforcement holds (19.2%). From these observations, we derive a 14-category enforcement gap taxonomy organized across manifest, code, platform, and architectural layers. Within our purposively selected corpus, observed enforcement outcomes differ substantially across interface categories: evaluated Activities and BroadcastReceivers exhibit a 100% gap rate, while ContentProviders, which benefit from framework-provided defenses such as setStrict() , achieve a 27.6% holds rate. We find that all seven evaluated platform compatibility changes with security intent are either disabled or gated at a targetSdkVersion that none of the applications in our evaluated corpus targets. We document 18 custom URI scheme registrations handling sensitive data (authentication tokens, payment credentials, medical information) despite the known unverifiability of custom schemes (RFC 8252 §8.1). Our study includes 23 positive controls, calibration cases demonstrating that the evaluation procedure distinguishes functioning enforcement from observed enforcement failures.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Android’s inter-process communication (IPC) architecture enables applications to expose functionality to other applications and to the system through four component types: Activities, Services, BroadcastReceivers, and ContentProviders. These components, along with custom URI scheme handlers, form the boundaries through which sensitive data and control flow cross between trust domains. The security of these boundaries depends on enforcement mechanisms at multiple levels: manifest-declared permissions, code-level caller identity checks, framework-provided input validation, and platform-level compatibility changes. Despite over a decade of research on Android IPC security, a fundamental question remains unanswered: does the enforcement at these boundaries actually work as designed? Existing research has addressed this question partially. Automated tools such as ComDroid [ 1 ] , CHEX [ 2 ] , and IccTA [ 3 ] detect specific vulnerability patterns at scale but do not evaluate enforcement holistically. Published security advisories document individual gaps but do not identify systemic patterns. Studies of user comprehension of the permission model [ 4 ] and compositional security analysis [ 5 ] evaluate aspects of the framework’s design but not its deployment at individual boundaries. We address this gap with a systematic evaluation comprising 120 security-enforcement evaluations in over 30 Google and AOSP packages on Android 17. Our approach differs from prior work in several ways. First, we frame each evaluation as a security-boundary assessment (does the enforcement mechanism at this boundary function as intended?) rather than a vulnerability detection exercise. Second, we report both enforcement gaps (where observed behavior diverges from expected) and enforcement holds (where enforcement works as designed), providing calibration cases that demonstrate the evaluation procedure can distinguish functioning enforcement from failures. Third, we evaluate enforcement across five inter-component interface categories and platform security controls in a single study, enabling cross-category comparison.

sections.heading: Research questions.
sections.text: RQ1: How does effective security enforcement vary across Android inter-component interfaces in a purposively selected corpus of first-party applications? RQ2: What recurring implementation and architectural patterns explain divergence between intended and observed security enforcement? RQ3: Are interface categories with framework-provided security defenses associated with different observed enforcement outcomes than categories that rely primarily on application-level checks?

sections.heading: Contributions.
sections.text: 1. Expected-versus-observed framework. A methodology for evaluating IPC boundary enforcement that determines expected behavior from documentation, sibling comparison, and platform design intent, then tests observed behavior through proof-of-concept applications and code review (Section 3 ). 2. 120 evaluations with 23 positive controls. Security-enforcement evaluations across Activities (27), ContentProviders (29), BroadcastReceivers (11), Services (14), custom URI schemes (18), platform security controls (10), and 11 separately evaluated well-defended components. Of the 120, 23 demonstrate functioning enforcement, serving as calibration cases (Section 4 ). 3. 14-category enforcement gap taxonomy. A taxonomy derived from evidence, organized across manifest, code, platform, and architectural layers (Section 5 ). 4. Platform compatibility change audit. An empirical evaluation of whether Android’s IPC-related compatibility changes are enforced on a shipping device, finding all seven disabled or unenforced on the test device (Section 4.7 ). 5. Cross-category enforcement comparison. Evidence that observed enforcement outcomes differ substantially across interface categories, with categories offering framework-provided defenses showing higher holds rates (Section 6 ). The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section 2 provides background on Android IPC and the permission model. Section 3 describes our threat model and methodology. Section 4 presents results. Section 5 derives the enforcement gap taxonomy. Section 6 discusses implications and threats to validity. Section 7 surveys related work. Section 8 concludes.

sections.heading: 2.1 Android IPC Components
sections.text: Android applications expose functionality through four component types, each with distinct IPC semantics: Activities are user-interface screens launched via startActivity() . An exported Activity can be launched by any application, receiving attacker-controlled data through Intent extras. Services provide background processing, accessed via bindService() or startService() . Bound services expose AIDL interfaces for inter-process method calls. BroadcastReceivers respond to system-wide or application-specific broadcast messages. A receiver processes attacker-controlled data from the broadcast Intent. ContentProviders expose structured data through a SQL-like query interface ( query() , insert() , update() , delete() ) and through file access ( openFile() ) and provider-defined method calls ( call() ). Callers supply selection predicates, projections, and sort orders that the provider incorporates into database queries.

sections.heading: 2.2 Android Permission Model
sections.text: Android controls component access through permissions at several protection levels: normal (auto-granted at install), dangerous (requires user approval), signature (same-certificate apps only), and signature|privileged (platform-signed or privileged partition). Components declare access requirements through manifest attributes: android:permission for Activities, Services, and BroadcastReceivers; android:readPermission and android:writePermission for ContentProviders. An android:permission declared at the application level provides a default permission to all components unless individually overridden.

sections.heading: 2.3 Component Export and Intent Resolution
sections.text: A component with android:exported="true" (or, for applications targeting API levels below 31, implicitly exported by declaring an intent filter) is accessible to any application. The android:exported attribute controls visibility; the android:permission attribute controls authorization. A component that is exported without a permission attribute is accessible to any application without restriction, unless a default permission is set at the application level.

sections.heading: 2.4 ContentProvider Query Defenses
sections.text: Android provides framework-level defenses for ContentProvider query injection. These are methods of SQLiteQueryBuilder and must be explicitly enabled by the developer: setStrict(true) checks the selection for injected clauses and, together with a projection map, rejects requested columns that are not in that map; setStrictColumns(true) verifies that projections and inserted or updated values contain only columns defined in the projection map; and setStrictGrammar(true) rejects selection and sort-order clauses that contain unexpected SQL keywords or tokens, such as subqueries. The compatibility change ENFORCE_STRICT_QUERY_BUILDER (ChangeId 143231523) was introduced to enable SQLiteQueryBuilder validation for specific ContentProvider queries; its documented scope covers CalendarProvider2 query selections.

sections.heading: 2.5 Custom URI Schemes and App Links
sections.text: Applications can register custom URI schemes (e.g., otpauth:// , gpay:// ) in their manifest intent-filters. Unlike HTTPS App Links, which support domain verification via android:autoVerify , custom URI schemes cannot be verified by the platform. Any application can register a handler for any custom scheme, enabling potential interception. RFC 8252 §8.1 [ 7 ] documents this limitation and recommends Proof Key for Code Exchange (PKCE) for public native clients, so that an intercepted authorization code cannot be redeemed by the interceptor.

sections.heading: 2.6 Platform Compatibility Framework
sections.text: Android’s Compatibility Framework introduces behavioral changes gated by the target application’s targetSdkVersion . Changes can be globally enabled, globally disabled, or conditionally enabled for applications targeting a minimum SDK version. This mechanism is intended for gradual adoption of breaking changes, including security hardening.

sections.heading: 3.1 Attacker Model
sections.text: We adopt a zero-permission app attacker model. The attacker is a malicious application installed on the same device as the target, holding zero runtime or manifest permissions beyond those automatically granted at install time (normal-level permissions). The attacker can: install via standard channels, send explicit intents to any exported component, query any exported ContentProvider, register intent filters for any custom URI scheme, and bind to any exported Service without android:permission . On Android 14 and later, Background Activity Launch (BAL) restrictions prevent background applications from starting Activities; all dynamic Activity evaluations in this study were executed from a visible foreground Activity in the proof-of-concept application, which reflects a realistic attacker capability. The attacker cannot: hold signature-level or privileged permissions, modify the system partition, exploit kernel-level vulnerabilities, or interact with non-exported components (unless granted temporary URI permission). Two further ContentProvider observations need capabilities beyond this model and are therefore excluded from the 120 evaluations. First, SettingsProvider skips its per-key read restriction for applications marked test-only, but such an application can be installed only through the Android Debug Bridge ( adb install -t ). Second, Drive’s StorageBackendContentProvider correctly rejects ordinary applications (counted as a hold, CP-18 in Section 4.3 ) but is reachable from the ADB shell, whose user holds the required MANAGE_DOCUMENTS permission.

sections.heading: 3.2 Evaluation Categories
sections.text: We organize evaluations into five inter-component interface categories and one platform security-control category (Figure 1 ): • B1 (Activity launch): Does the target Activity verify the caller before processing attacker-controlled extras? • B2 (ContentProvider query): Does the provider validate query parameters and enforce access control? • B3 (Broadcast delivery): Does the receiver verify the sender before acting on broadcast data? • B4 (Service binding): Does the service verify the caller’s identity and authorization? • B5 (URI scheme): Can the platform verify which app should handle a given custom URI scheme? • B6 (Platform controls): Are platform-level security hardening mechanisms active on the test device? B1–B5 evaluate enforcement at inter-component interfaces. B6 evaluates platform security guardrails that are intended to reinforce component-level enforcement; these are not IPC boundaries themselves but platform-level controls with security intent. Solid arrows: direct IPC (B1–B4). Dashed: URI scheme interception (B5). B6 covers platform controls.

sections.heading: 3.3 Expected-Versus-Observed Framework
sections.text: For each evaluation, we determine the expected enforcement from one or more sources, listed from strongest to weakest: (1) explicit platform or security specification, (2) Android developer documentation specifying the intended behavior, (3) protection level semantics, where a permission’s level does not match the sensitivity of the protected resource, (4) sibling comparison, where a component’s siblings in the same manifest implement a security mechanism but the evaluated component does not. We determine the observed enforcement through: dynamic testing (PoC app execution on a Pixel 6a running Android 17, with logcat capture), static analysis (manifest analysis and code review of decompiled APKs or AOSP source), or both. Each evaluation is classified as a GAP (observed behavior diverges from expected enforcement) or HOLDS (enforcement works as designed). Evidence is tagged as S (static only), D (dynamic only), or S+D (both). Each evaluation carries an identifier whose prefix names its category: A (Activity), CP (ContentProvider), BR (BroadcastReceiver), SV (Service), URI (custom URI scheme), SYS (platform control), and NEG (well-defended component used as a positive control). For example, CP-06 is the sixth ContentProvider evaluation. Section 4 discusses evaluations in functional groups and cites these identifiers so that each statement can be matched to a specific evaluation, and Appendix A lists all 120 evaluations by identifier with the component, package, outcome, and evidence type. Identifiers are numbered consecutively within each category, except that ContentProvider identifiers run to CP-34 although 29 are counted: three duplicate positive controls NEG-06 to NEG-08, and two require ADB access (Section 3.1 ). Figure 2 summarizes the study workflow. 1. Select component and evaluation category 2. Determine expected enforcement 3. Test observed enforcement (PoC / code review) 4. Classify outcome: GAP or HOLDS 5. Assign taxonomy category (T1–T4) 6. Record evidence type (S, D, or S+D) specification, docs, sibling comparison Figure 2: Per-evaluation workflow. Steps 2–6 are applied to each of the 120 evaluations. Expected enforcement is derived from specification, documentation, protection-level semantics, or sibling comparison.

sections.heading: 3.4 Evaluation Scope
sections.text: In scope: Android phone inter-component interfaces on a Google Pixel 6a running Android 17 (API 37, builds CP2A.260605.012 and CP31.260608.007). Google and AOSP first-party applications, including Chrome and Fitbit. Out of scope: Wear OS components (separate security model), kernel/Binder-layer analysis (below the IPC abstraction), network-level attacks, and WebView/JavaScript bridge security, with one exception (SYS-10, Section 4.7 ).

sections.heading: 3.5 Limitations of Methodology
sections.text: Our evaluations are not randomly sampled; the researcher selected boundaries based on judgment about where gaps might exist, biasing the gap rate upward. The 80.8% gap rate characterizes the evaluated corpus, not all Android IPC boundaries. Twenty-one evaluations (17.5%) are based on static analysis only and lack runtime confirmation. Evaluations cover a single device (Pixel 6a) and Android version (17). The study focuses on Google/AOSP first-party apps; findings may not generalize to the broader Android app ecosystem. App versions are as installed at evaluation time; Google apps receive frequent updates.

sections.heading: 4 Results
sections.text: Throughout this section, identifiers in parentheses, such as (CP-06) or (A-12), point to individual evaluations; Appendix A gives the full entry for each.

sections.heading: 4.2 Activity Boundary Findings (B1)
sections.text: All 27 evaluated Activity boundaries exhibit enforcement gaps, spanning eight functional groups. OAuth/authentication callbacks (A-01–A-03). Three authentication callback Activities in Gmail and GMS accept arbitrary callers. CseRedirectUriReceiverActivity (Gmail) processes OAuth callback data from any application. BrowserSignInResponseHandlerActivity (GMS) handles Firebase Auth callbacks on both HTTPS and HTTP schemes without origin verification. AuthzenDeeplinkHandlerActivity (GMS) handles sign-in challenge links without verifying the caller. Payment Activities (A-04–A-07). Four Activities in Google Wallet and GMS handle payment-related operations without adequate caller verification. FinishAndroidAppRedirectProxyActivity forwards caller-controlled URLs through GMS’s process context. AddNewCardThroughBrowserActivity accepts card-tokenization requests from any caller. PresentationModeActivity activates NFC tap-to-pay without lock screen authentication. Wallet’s DeepLinkActivity declares android:autoVerify , but that attribute only governs implicit intents, so any application can open its deep-link routes with an explicit intent. Credential and identity Activities (A-08, A-09). SharePasswordsActivity (GMS) accepts an arbitrary requesting agent name and package in its credential-sharing flow, and a diagnostics tool’s login Activity uses an authentication check that always succeeds. Debug Activities (A-10, A-11). CalendarDebugActivity runs in the CalendarProvider process, allowing any caller to bypass the READ_CALENDAR permission check. ContactsDumpActivity zips and serves the entire contacts data directory without access control. Confused deputy (A-12–A-17). Six Activities act on a caller’s behalf with privileges the caller lacks, the confused deputy pattern [ 12 ] . Three render protected data directly: LaunchInfoActivity renders calendar events without requiring READ_CALENDAR , QuickContactActivity renders full contact cards without READ_CONTACTS , and HostPhotoPagerActivity renders photos without READ_MEDIA_IMAGES . Three relay caller-controlled requests under the target application’s identity: BetterBug’s DispatchActivity forwards intents to an Activity protected by the DUMP permission (A-15), SystemUI’s MediaProjectionPermissionActivity reads the package name for its consent-reuse check from an attacker-controlled extra when the caller is unknown (A-16, static evidence), and a Play Store Activity forwards a caller-controlled URI from the Play Store process (A-17, static evidence). DoS and inconsistent validation (A-18–A-23). Five Activities crash when they receive empty or malformed Intents, causing process-level denial of service (A-18, A-20–A-23). KeyChainActivity (A-20) crashes the system-UID process; BrightnessDialog (A-22) crashes the main SystemUI process. In the same group, a Dialer handler (A-19) is the only one of its sibling handlers that omits the Google signature check the others apply. PII exposure and privileged configuration (A-24–A-27). An emergency-information screen designed for the lock screen is exported to any application and exposes the owner’s name, medical information, and emergency contacts (A-24). Three Activities perform privileged configuration without the permission their context implies: a Wi-Fi calling activation screen whose sibling Activities require MODIFY_PHONE_STATE (A-25), an eSIM download screen that accepts a forced-provisioning flag from any caller (A-26), and a parental-controls setup Activity reachable without a manifest permission (A-27, static evidence).

sections.heading: 4.3 ContentProvider Boundary Findings (B2)
sections.text: Of 29 evaluated ContentProvider boundaries, 21 exhibit gaps and 8 exhibit holds, the highest holds rate of any interface category. SQL injection (CP-01–CP-13). CalendarProvider2 accepts unsanitized input in its selection, projection, and write-path (update and delete) parameters, permitting cross-table data extraction (CP-01–CP-03), and the platform change that would enforce strict query validation for it is disabled (CP-04; see SYS-01). Selection injection also reaches ContactsProvider2, CallLogProvider, and CarrierIdProvider, the last with full UNION injection and no permission required (CP-05, CP-07, CP-08); sortOrder injection affects four providers (CP-09); and CellBroadcastContentProvider applies none of the strict-mode checks (CP-10, static evidence). Where the defenses are applied, they hold: ContactsProvider2 blocks projection injection via setStrict(true) (CP-06), CalendarProvider2’s instances query enables all three strict-mode checks (CP-11), and MediaProvider and DownloadProvider reject SQL keywords in sortOrder (CP-12, CP-13). Shared library gap (CP-14–CP-19). Four Google Workspace applications (Drive, Docs, Sheets, Slides) share a LegacyStorageBackendContentProvider with zero permission checks on query() (CP-14–CP-17). The modern StorageBackendContentProvider in the same packages correctly requires MANAGE_DOCUMENTS (CP-18, HOLDS), and the legacy provider’s openFile() resists path traversal because it looks files up by database identifier rather than building a filesystem path from the request (CP-19, HOLDS). Asymmetric permissions (CP-23, CP-24). MmsSmsProvider declares readPermission but no writePermission , allowing deletion of SMS/MMS records. GoogleSettingsProvider declares writePermission but no readPermission , exposing 18 partner settings. Other provider gaps (CP-20–CP-22, CP-25, CP-27, CP-34). A debug provider serves a ZIP archive of the contacts database (CP-20); Settings’ SuggestionStateProvider reveals screen-lock and biometric enrollment status (CP-21); Messages’ AvatarContentProvider proxies arbitrary content:// URIs under its own READ_CONTACTS permission (CP-22); ServiceStateProvider skips its permission checks for callers targeting API levels below 31 (CP-25); GServicesProvider is guarded only by a normal-level permission while exposing 1,404 configuration entries (CP-27); and a temporary URI grant from the contact picker permits SQL injection that reaches all internal ContactsProvider2 tables (CP-34). Of the identifiers CP-28 to CP-33, three duplicate positive controls (CP-28 to CP-30) and one falls outside the attacker model (CP-33, Section 3.1 ). The other two are counted holds: BluetoothOppProvider applies setStrict(true) and a path permission (CP-31), and the phone application’s SIM contact providers require contacts permissions (CP-32).

sections.heading: 4.4 BroadcastReceiver Boundary Findings (B3)
sections.text: All 11 evaluated BroadcastReceiver boundaries exhibit gaps. GmsExternalReceiver (BR-01–BR-03). GMS uses a single exported receiver for 31 distinct Intent actions with no android:permission and no per-action sender validation (BR-03). Behind it, FrpUpdateIntentOperation writes the Factory Reset Protection (FRP) secret without sender verification (BR-01), and AuthZenEventHandler forces re-registration of six CryptAuth security keys (BR-02). Debug receivers (BR-04–BR-06). TestingToolsBroadcastReceiver is present in 11 Google applications, gated by a runtime Phenotype flag (Google’s server-controlled feature-flag system) rather than stripped at build time (BR-04). CalendarProvider’s debug receiver responds to a secret-code broadcast (BR-05), and a test receiver in com.google.android.apps.scone forwards simulated state changes to a privileged service (BR-06). Safety-critical receiver (BR-08). CrisisNotificationBroadcastReceiver accepts broadcast intents from any application, enabling dismissal of earthquake, tsunami, and active shooter alerts. Other receivers (BR-07, BR-09–BR-11). SystemUI’s media-output dialog action is not declared as a protected broadcast although its sibling action is (BR-07); an OMA-DM receiver without a permission invokes a permission-protected receiver directly as a Java method, bypassing the system’s broadcast permission check (BR-09); Wallet receivers let any application cancel Wallet notifications, including fraud alerts (BR-10); and the Messages RCS provisioning receiver relies on a normal-level permission and validates the sender for only one of its seven actions (BR-11).

sections.heading: 4.5 Service Boundary Findings (B4)
sections.text: Of 14 evaluated Service boundaries, 10 exhibit gaps and 4 exhibit holds. MediaBrowserService pattern (SV-01, SV-02). YouTube’s MediaBrowserService only blocks SystemUI, accepting all other callers with zero permissions. Bluetooth’s MediaBrowserService accepts all callers with zero validation. Missing or weak service permissions (SV-03–SV-06, SV-09, SV-10). GMS exports 126 services without android:permission (SV-03), and Photos exports seven backup services without permission while keeping its internal backup services unexported (SV-04). Messages and the Google app guard services with normal-level permissions that every application receives automatically (SV-05, SV-10). FederatedCompute performs no Binder caller checks anywhere in its service (SV-06), and an on-device personalization service lacks the permission its sibling service requires (SV-09). Inconsistent AIDL enforcement (SV-07, SV-08). KeyChainService exposes approximately 50 Binder methods; 5 lack caller identity checks, allowing enumeration of 120 system certificate authority (CA) certificate aliases. NfcService protects all but 2 of approximately 50 methods; the two unprotected methods accept forged host card emulation (HCE) data. Positive controls (SV-11–SV-14). FelicaServiceImpl enforces getCallingUid() (SV-11). ZeroPartyBinder performs UID plus signature verification (SV-12). NfcService enforces NFC permissions on all its other methods (SV-13). Two GMS services throw SecurityException on unprivileged bind attempts (SV-14).

sections.heading: 4.6 Custom URI Scheme Findings (B5)
sections.text: We identified 18 custom URI scheme registrations handling security-sensitive data (URI-01 to URI-18); where one application registers several related schemes for the same purpose, such as tez:// and gpay:// in Google Pay, they form a single evaluation. Table 3 lists selected schemes. All 18 share the same architectural exposure: Android cannot verify which application should handle a custom scheme [ 7 ] , meaning any installed application can register a competing handler for any of these schemes. sections.heading: 4.7 Platform Security-Control Findings (B6)
sections.text: All 10 platform-level evaluations exhibit gaps. Compatibility changes (SYS-01–SYS-07). We evaluated seven Android compatibility framework changes with security intent (Table 4 ). On our test device (Pixel 6a, Android 17), three changes are disabled and four are gated at targetSdkVersion=37 , which none of the applications in our evaluated corpus targets. Some of these changes may have different documented default states; our observations reflect the state observed via am compat get-config on the test device. A Settings Tile Parcelable implementation writes and reads fields in different orders, enabling a self-changing Bundle attack. This class of vulnerability (Parcelable serialization/deserialization mismatch) was previously identified in CVE-2023-45777 [ 8 ] ; our observation represents a similar pattern on a current platform build. The platform defense ( PARCEL_HARDENING ) is gated at targetSdk=37 on the test device and thus unenforced. Third-party library proxy execution (SYS-09). InCallController in system_server uses createPackageContext() with flag 3 ( CONTEXT_INCLUDE_CODE | CONTEXT_IGNORE_SECURITY ) against an attacker-controlled package during getInCallServiceComponents enumeration, triggered by any app holding the auto-granted MANAGE_OWN_CALLS permission. According to the original report, this loads code from the attacker’s Dalvik Executable (DEX) into system_server (UID 1000), enabling arbitrary code execution without user interaction. This vulnerability was discovered and reported by sithi [ 10 ] , assigned CVE-2026-49881 [ 9 ] , and patched in the September 2026 Android Security Bulletin. We did not rediscover it; we include it because our static review confirmed that the vulnerable code path is present in the evaluated builds, which predate that patch. Our search for the same pattern elsewhere found only uses that resolve to Google-signed packages in application context (NEG-09, NEG-10). JavaScript bridge (SYS-10). The one WebView-related evaluation in scope concerns a JavaScript bridge in Google Maps whose openUrl() method turns script-supplied URLs into native intent launches within the Maps process. This evaluation rests on static evidence only; we did not confirm that an attacker can inject script into the relevant WebView.

sections.heading: 4.8 Positive Controls
sections.text: Twenty-three evaluations demonstrate enforcement holds, providing calibration cases that confirm the evaluation procedure can detect functioning enforcement. Well-defended components (NEG-01–NEG-11). These eleven evaluations target components chosen as positive controls rather than as suspected gaps. Pixel Launcher uses signature permissions combined with SHA-256 package allowlists (NEG-01). The NFC stack uses flag 0 for createPackageContext , avoids FLAG_MUTABLE for PendingIntents, and enforces permissions on all Binder methods (NEG-03). ManagedProvisioning performs multi-factor code-level caller verification despite being exported without a manifest permission (NEG-04). The strongest of these components combine manifest-level permissions, code-level caller validation, and explicit allowlists. ContentProvider and Service defenses. The eight ContentProvider holds and four Service holds are described in Sections 4.3 and 4.5 . Table 5 lists all 23 holds with the mechanism that held in each case. sections.heading: 5 Enforcement Gap Taxonomy
sections.text: From the 97 enforcement gaps, we derive a taxonomy of 14 enforcement failure patterns organized across four layers. The taxonomy groups patterns by where in the enforcement stack the failure occurs; we note that individual categories represent different kinds of entities (implementation errors, deployment states, architectural limitations) unified by their shared effect of producing an observed enforcement gap. sections.heading: Pattern co-occurrence.
sections.text: Several evaluations exhibit multiple patterns simultaneously. CalendarProvider2 (CP-01–CP-04) exhibits both SQL injection (T2.1) and a disabled platform defense (T3.1). The Google Workspace legacy providers (CP-14–CP-17) exhibit SQL injection (T2.1) compounded with feature-flag-gated fixes (T3.2). The Play Store redirect Activity (A-17) and the TestingToolsBroadcastReceiver debug receiver (BR-04) each combine their primary pattern with a flag-gated fix (T3.2), ServiceStateProvider (CP-25) combines a missing permission with SDK-conditional checks (T3.3), and the Settings Tile Parcelable regression (SYS-08) exhibits Parcelable mismatch (T3.4) with the defending compat change, PARCEL_HARDENING , unenforced (T3.1).

sections.heading: 6.1 Summary of Findings by Research Question
sections.text: RQ1 (enforcement variation across interfaces): Within our purposively selected corpus, observed enforcement outcomes differ substantially across interface categories. Activities and BroadcastReceivers exhibit 100% gap rates among evaluated boundaries, while ContentProviders and Services show holds rates of 27.6% and 28.6% (Section 6.2 ). RQ2 (recurring patterns): The 14-category taxonomy identifies three dominant patterns: missing authorization (T1.1, 35 instances), URI scheme unverifiability (T4.1, 18), and SQL injection (T2.1, 13), accounting for 68% of observed gaps (Section 5 ). RQ3 (framework-provided defenses): Interface categories where the framework offers per-request enforcement primitives are associated with higher holds rates: ContentProviders ( setStrict family, separate readPermission / writePermission ) at 27.6% and Services (per-call Binder caller identity) at 28.6%, compared with 0% for evaluated Activities and BroadcastReceivers (Section 6.2 ).

sections.heading: 6.2 Framework-Provided Defenses and Enforcement Outcomes
sections.text: Within our corpus, evaluated Activities and BroadcastReceivers show a 100% gap rate, while ContentProviders and Services show 72.4% and 71.4%. ContentProviders benefit from framework-provided defenses that developers can opt into: the three strict-mode methods of SQLiteQueryBuilder (Section 2.4 ) and separate manifest attributes for read and write permissions. When developers apply these mechanisms, enforcement holds: in ContactsProvider2, in CalendarProvider2’s instances query, in MediaProvider and DownloadProvider, and in BluetoothOppProvider (CP-06, CP-11–CP-13, CP-31). Services offer a different primitive: every Binder call carries the caller’s identity, which the service can check with getCallingUid() or enforceCallingPermission() , and three of the four Service holds, FelicaServiceImpl, ZeroPartyBinder, and NfcService, rely on such checks (SV-11–SV-13). Activities, by contrast, have no comparable framework-level caller verification mechanism: the receiving Activity is not told who started it unless the caller cooperates, and there is no framework validator for Intent extras analogous to setStrict() . We observe an association between the availability of framework-provided defenses and better enforcement outcomes. A supplementary triage of all 376 Google and AOSP packages on the test device (encompassing 3,721 exported components) identified zero exported ContentProviders lacking access controls beyond those already in our corpus; each was secured through signature-certificate allowlists, calling-package verification, or runtime permission enforcement. This broader observation is consistent with the finding that ContentProvider enforcement benefits from framework-provided defenses that other categories lack. However, we note that this comparison is not controlled: the interface categories differ in many ways beyond framework support (API semantics, developer population, selection criteria), so we cannot establish a causal relationship from this data alone.

sections.heading: 6.3 The Compatibility Change Paradox
sections.text: On our test device, all seven evaluated platform compatibility changes with security intent are either disabled or gated at a targetSdkVersion that none of the applications in our evaluated corpus targets. The platform team recognized each problem, wrote a fix, and shipped it in the platform code; however, on this device, those fixes are not enforced. This creates a gap between the intended security behavior documented in the platform code and the actual enforcement observed on the device. The targetSdkVersion gating mechanism creates an enforcement lag, and the same mechanism appears inside applications: ServiceStateProvider applies its permission checks only to callers targeting API 31 or later (CP-25), so an attacker application avoids them simply by declaring an older target such as API 28. This is compounded at the app level: CalendarProvider2 has SQL injection (CP-01), and the platform defense that would catch it, the ENFORCE_STRICT_QUERY_BUILDER compatibility change, is disabled on the test device (SYS-01).

sections.heading: 6.4 Custom URI Schemes: Systematic Reuse of a Known-Vulnerable Pattern
sections.text: RFC 8252 §8.1, published in October 2017, documents that custom URI scheme redirect URIs are vulnerable to interception and recommends PKCE for public native clients. Despite this, we document 18 custom URI scheme registrations handling sensitive data across 15+ packages. The persistence of custom schemes nine years after the RFC suggests that awareness of an architectural limitation does not prevent its systematic reuse, particularly when the secure alternative (HTTPS App Links) requires additional infrastructure. We classify these as architectural exposure rather than necessarily exploitable vulnerabilities, since individual applications may implement compensating controls (e.g., PKCE, state validation).

sections.heading: 6.5 Shared Code as Enforcement Gap Amplifier
sections.text: A single shared library places LegacyStorageBackendContentProvider in four Google Workspace applications, each with the same missing permission check (CP-14–CP-17). TestingToolsBroadcastReceiver is present in 11 applications (BR-04). A single code-level gap in a shared library produces multiple affected applications. Conversely, a single fix in the shared library would remediate all.

sections.heading: 6.6 The Catch-All Anti-Pattern
sections.text: GmsExternalReceiver handles 31 Intent actions through a single exported receiver with no android:permission . This concentrates authorization at the per-action handler level, but at least two handlers perform no caller validation. In contrast, Pixel Launcher uses per-provider signature permissions with SHA-256 allowlists (NEG-01).

sections.heading: 6.7 What Distinguishes Well-Defended Components
sections.text: Across the 23 enforcement holds (Table 5 ), enforcement rests on four kinds of mechanism: (1) manifest-level permissions at signature or signature|privileged level, (2) code-level caller identity checks, (3) explicit package or signature allowlists rather than general permission checks, and (4) framework input validation. The most robust components, such as Pixel Launcher and the NFC stack, combine several of these, applying code-level checks even where a manifest permission is already present. Others were evaluated for a single mechanism, such as the sortOrder validation in MediaProvider and DownloadProvider.

sections.heading: 6.8 Threats to Validity
sections.text: Selection bias. Evaluations are not randomly sampled; the 80.8% gap rate characterizes the evaluated corpus, not all Android IPC boundaries. These observations motivate a broader measurement study with systematic or random sampling. Single device and version. All evaluations use Pixel 6a running Android 17; compatibility change states may differ on other devices or builds. Static-only evidence. 21 evaluations (17.5%) lack runtime confirmation. Google/AOSP focus. Third-party app enforcement patterns may differ. Temporal validity. Specific gaps may be fixed after our evaluation window. Confounding factors. The observed association between framework-provided defenses and enforcement outcomes (RQ3) is not a controlled comparison; interface categories differ in multiple dimensions beyond framework support.

sections.heading: 7 Related Work
sections.text: Android IPC security tools. ComDroid [ 1 ] introduced static analysis for inter-application communication vulnerabilities and examined 20 applications in detail. CHEX [ 2 ] extended this with data-flow analysis for component hijacking across 5,486 apps. IccTA [ 3 ] performed ICC-aware taint analysis. AceDroid [ 6 ] detected inconsistent access control checks. These tools detect specific patterns at scale; we complement this with a holistic enforcement evaluation that includes positive controls, cross-category comparison, and platform-level assessment. Permission model studies. Felt et al. [ 4 ] studied how users attend to, comprehend, and respond to Android permission prompts. Bagheri et al. [ 5 ] developed COVERT, a compositional analysis framework for detecting inter-app permission leakage. Our work evaluates enforcement of the existing permission model at individual boundaries rather than analyzing the model’s design or user comprehension. ContentProvider security. Zhou and Jiang [ 11 ] detected passive content leaks and content pollution through exported ContentProviders, finding 2.3% of 62,519 applications susceptible. We extend this with evaluation of the full enforcement chain: app-level injection, framework-level defenses ( setStrict ), and platform-level compatibility changes. Confused deputy in Android. Felt et al. [ 12 ] defined the permission re-delegation attack model and proposed IPC Inspection. Grace et al. [ 13 ] showed that preloaded applications on stock Android phones leak permission-protected capabilities through exported components. Bugiel et al. [ 14 ] proposed XManDroid for cross-app IPC monitoring. We contribute concrete evaluations in current (2026) first-party applications, showing the pattern persists. URI scheme security. RFC 8252 §8.1 [ 7 ] documents the custom URI scheme interception risk. To our knowledge, among the studies we reviewed, no prior work provides a systematic survey of custom URI scheme usage across a major first-party app ecosystem; we document 18 scheme registrations handling sensitive data despite the known risk. sections.heading: 8 Conclusion
sections.text: We presented a systematic study comprising 120 security-enforcement evaluations across five Android inter-component interface categories and platform security controls. Our expected-versus-observed framework evaluates enforcement as a security-boundary assessment, reporting both gaps (97) and holds (23). The 14-category enforcement gap taxonomy organizes failures across manifest, code, platform, and architectural layers, with three dominant patterns: missing authorization (T1.1), URI scheme unverifiability (T4.1), and SQL injection (T2.1), accounting for 68% of observed gaps (RQ2). Three findings stand out. First, within our purposively selected corpus, observed enforcement outcomes differ substantially across interface categories (RQ1), and categories with framework-provided enforcement primitives are associated with higher holds rates (RQ3): ContentProviders and Services have holds rates of 27.6% and 28.6%, while Activities and BroadcastReceivers have 0% among evaluated boundaries. This observation motivates investigation into whether providing stronger framework-level enforcement defaults across all IPC types would improve outcomes. Second, all seven evaluated platform compatibility changes with security intent are disabled or unenforced on the test device, creating a gap between the platform team’s intentions and actual enforcement. Third, 18 custom URI scheme registrations handle sensitive data despite a nine-year-old RFC documenting the interception risk. Our positive controls demonstrate that effective enforcement is achievable: the best-defended components combine manifest permissions, code-level caller checks, and explicit allowlists. The gap is not in the availability of enforcement mechanisms but in their consistent application.

sections.heading: Ethical Considerations
sections.text: All evaluations were performed on the researcher’s own device (Google Pixel 6a). No user data was accessed or exfiltrated. Dynamic evaluations used proof-of-concept applications on the researcher’s own accounts. This study analyzes the design and behavior of publicly available system components; all observations are derived from manifest inspection, publicly available source code (AOSP), and standard IPC interactions on a researcher-controlled device.

We present a systematic study of security enforcement comprising 120 evaluations (99 inter-component interface evaluations across five interface categories, 10 platform security-control evaluations, and 11 dedicated positive controls) in over 30 Google and AOSP packages on Android 17 (API 37). Using an expected-versus-observed framework under a zero-permission attacker model, we evaluate whether each boundary’s enforcement mechanism functions as designed. We find 97 enforcement gaps (80.8%) and 23 enforcement holds (19.2%). From these observations, we derive a 14-category enforcement gap taxonomy organized across manifest, code, platform, and architectural layers. Within our purposively selected corpus, observed enforcement outcomes differ substantially across interface categories: evaluated Activities and BroadcastReceivers exhibit a 100% gap rate, while ContentProviders, which benefit from framework-provided defenses such as setStrict() , achieve a 27.6% holds rate. We find that all seven evaluated platform compatibility changes with security intent are either disabled or gated at a targetSdkVersion that none of the applications in our evaluated corpus targets. We document 18 custom URI scheme registrations handling sensitive data (authentication tokens, payment credentials, medical information) despite the known unverifiability of custom schemes (RFC 8252 §8.1). Our study includes 23 positive controls, calibration cases demonstrating that the evaluation procedure distinguishes functioning enforcement from observed enforcement failures. These components, along with custom URI scheme handlers, form the boundaries through which sensitive data and control flow cross between trust domains. The security of these boundaries depends on enforcement mechanisms at multiple levels: manifest-declared permissions, code-level caller identity checks, framework-provided input validation, and platform-level compatibility changes. Despite over a decade of research on Android IPC security, a fundamental question remains unanswered: does the enforcement at these boundaries actually work as designed? Existing research has addressed this question partially. Automated tools such as ComDroid [ 1 ] , CHEX [ 2 ] , and IccTA [ 3 ] detect specific vulnerability patterns at scale but do not evaluate enforcement holistically. Published security advisories document individual gaps but do not identify systemic patterns. Studies of user comprehension of the permission model [ 4 ] and compositional security analysis [ 5 ] evaluate aspects of the framework’s design but not its deployment at individual boundaries. We address this gap with a systematic evaluation comprising 120 security-enforcement evaluations in over 30 Google and AOSP packages on Android 17. Our approach differs from prior work in several ways. First, we frame each evaluation as a security-boundary assessment (does the enforcement mechanism at this boundary function as intended?) rather than a vulnerability detection exercise. Second, we report both enforcement gaps (where observed behavior diverges from expected) and enforcement holds (where enforcement works as designed), providing calibration cases that demonstrate the evaluation procedure can distinguish functioning enforcement from failures. Third, we evaluate enforcement across five inter-component interface categories and platform security controls in a single study, enabling cross-category comparison. Research questions. RQ1: How does effective security enforcement vary across Android inter-component interfaces in a purposively selected corpus of first-party applications? RQ2: What recurring implementation and architectural patterns explain divergence between intended and observed security enforcement? RQ3: Are interface categories with framework-provided security defenses associated with different observed enforcement outcomes than categories that rely primarily on application-level checks? Contributions. 1. Expected-versus-observed framework. A methodology for evaluating IPC boundary enforcement that determines expected behavior from documentation, sibling comparison, and platform design intent, then tests observed behavior through proof-of-concept applications and code review (Section 3 ). 2. 120 evaluations with 23 positive controls. Security-enforcement evaluations across Activities (27), ContentProviders (29), BroadcastReceivers (11), Services (14), custom URI schemes (18), platform security controls (10), and 11 separately evaluated well-defended components. Of the 120, 23 demonstrate functioning enforcement, serving as calibration cases (Section 4 ). 3. 14-category enforcement gap taxonomy. A taxonomy derived from evidence, organized across manifest, code, platform, and architectural layers (Section 5 ). 4. Platform compatibility change audit. An empirical evaluation of whether Android’s IPC-related compatibility changes are enforced on a shipping device, finding all seven disabled or unenforced on the test device (Section 4.7 ). 5. Cross-category enforcement comparison. Evidence that observed enforcement outcomes differ substantially across interface categories, with categories offering framework-provided defenses showing higher holds rates (Section 6 ). The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section 2 provides background on Android IPC and the permission model. Section 3 describes our threat model and methodology. Section 4 presents results. Section 5 derives the enforcement gap taxonomy. Section 6 discusses implications and threats to validity. Section 7 surveys related work. Section 8 concludes. 2 Background 2.1 Android IPC Components Android applications expose functionality through four component types, each with distinct IPC semantics: Activities are user-interface screens launched via startActivity() . An exported Activity can be launched by any application, receiving attacker-controlled data through Intent extras. Services provide background processing, accessed via bindService() or startService() . Bound services expose AIDL interfaces for inter-process method calls. BroadcastReceivers respond to system-wide or application-specific broadcast messages. A receiver processes attacker-controlled data from the broadcast Intent. ContentProviders expose structured data through a SQL-like query interface ( query() , insert() , update() , delete() ) and through file access ( openFile() ) and provider-defined method calls ( call() ). Callers supply selection predicates, projections, and sort orders that the provider incorporates into database queries. 2.2 Android Permission Model Android controls component access through permissions at several protection levels: normal (auto-granted at install), dangerous (requires user approval), signature (same-certificate apps only), and signature|privileged (platform-signed or privileged partition). Components declare access requirements through manifest attributes: android:permission for Activities, Services, and BroadcastReceivers; android:readPermission and android:writePermission for ContentProviders. An android:permission declared at the application level provides a default permission to all components unless individually overridden. 2.3 Component Export and Intent Resolution A component with android:exported="true" (or, for applications targeting API levels below 31, implicitly exported by declaring an intent filter) is accessible to any application. The android:exported attribute controls visibility; the android:permission attribute controls authorization. A component that is exported without a permission attribute is accessible to any application without restriction, unless a default permission is set at the application level. 2.4 ContentProvider Query Defenses Android provides framework-level defenses for ContentProvider query injection. These are methods of SQLiteQueryBuilder and must be explicitly enabled by the developer: setStrict(true) checks the selection for injected clauses and, together with a projection map, rejects requested columns that are not in that map; setStrictColumns(true) verifies that projections and inserted or updated values contain only columns defined in the projection map; and setStrictGrammar(true) rejects selection and sort-order clauses that contain unexpected SQL keywords or tokens, such as subqueries. The compatibility change ENFORCE_STRICT_QUERY_BUILDER (ChangeId 143231523) was introduced to enable SQLiteQueryBuilder validation for specific ContentProvider queries; its documented scope covers CalendarProvider2 query selections. 2.5 Custom URI Schemes and App Links Applications can register custom URI schemes (e.g., otpauth:// , gpay:// ) in their manifest intent-filters. Unlike HTTPS App Links, which support domain verification via android:autoVerify , custom URI schemes cannot be verified by the platform. Any application can register a handler for any custom scheme, enabling potential interception. RFC 8252 §8.1 [ 7 ] documents this limitation and recommends Proof Key for Code Exchange (PKCE) for public native clients, so that an intercepted authorization code cannot be redeemed by the interceptor. 2.6 Platform Compatibility Framework Android’s Compatibility Framework introduces behavioral changes gated by the target application’s targetSdkVersion . Changes can be globally enabled, globally disabled, or conditionally enabled for applications targeting a minimum SDK version. This mechanism is intended for gradual adoption of breaking changes, including security hardening. 3 Threat Model and Methodology 3.1 Attacker Model We adopt a zero-permission app attacker model. The attacker is a malicious application installed on the same device as the target, holding zero runtime or manifest permissions beyond those automatically granted at install time (normal-level permissions). The attacker can: install via standard channels, send explicit intents to any exported component, query any exported ContentProvider, register intent filters for any custom URI scheme, and bind to any exported Service without android:permission . On Android 14 and later, Background Activity Launch (BAL) restrictions prevent background applications from starting Activities; all dynamic Activity evaluations in this study were executed from a visible foreground Activity in the proof-of-concept application, which reflects a realistic attacker capability. The attacker cannot: hold signature-level or privileged permissions, modify the system partition, exploit kernel-level vulnerabilities, or interact with non-exported components (unless granted temporary URI permission). Two further ContentProvider observations need capabilities beyond this model and are therefore excluded from the 120 evaluations. First, SettingsProvider skips its per-key read restriction for applications marked test-only, but such an application can be installed only through the Android Debug Bridge ( adb install -t ). Second, Drive’s StorageBackendContentProvider correctly rejects ordinary applications (counted as a hold, CP-18 in Section 4.3 ) but is reachable from the ADB shell, whose user holds the required MANAGE_DOCUMENTS permission. 3.2 Evaluation Categories We organize evaluations into five inter-component interface categories and one platform security-control category (Figure 1 ): • B1 (Activity launch): Does the target Activity verify the caller before processing attacker-controlled extras? • B2 (ContentProvider query): Does the provider validate query parameters and enforce access control? • B3 (Broadcast delivery): Does the receiver verify the sender before acting on broadcast data? • B4 (Service binding): Does the service verify the caller’s identity and authorization? • B5 (URI scheme): Can the platform verify which app should handle a given custom URI scheme? • B6 (Platform controls): Are platform-level security hardening mechanisms active on the test device? B1–B5 evaluate enforcement at inter-component interfaces. B6 evaluates platform security guardrails that are intended to reinforce component-level enforcement; these are not IPC boundaries themselves but platform-level controls with security intent. Solid arrows: direct IPC (B1–B4). Dashed: URI scheme interception (B5). B6 covers platform controls. 3.3 Expected-Versus-Observed Framework For each evaluation, we determine the expected enforcement from one or more sources, listed from strongest to weakest: (1) explicit platform or security specification, (2) Android developer documentation specifying the intended behavior, (3) protection level semantics, where a permission’s level does not match the sensitivity of the protected resource, (4) sibling comparison, where a component’s siblings in the same manifest implement a security mechanism but the evaluated component does not. We determine the observed enforcement through: dynamic testing (PoC app execution on a Pixel 6a running Android 17, with logcat capture), static analysis (manifest analysis and code review of decompiled APKs or AOSP source), or both. Each evaluation is classified as a GAP (observed behavior diverges from expected enforcement) or HOLDS (enforcement works as designed). Evidence is tagged as S (static only), D (dynamic only), or S+D (both). Each evaluation carries an identifier whose prefix names its category: A (Activity), CP (ContentProvider), BR (BroadcastReceiver), SV (Service), URI (custom URI scheme), SYS (platform control), and NEG (well-defended component used as a positive control). For example, CP-06 is the sixth ContentProvider evaluation. Section 4 discusses evaluations in functional groups and cites these identifiers so that each statement can be matched to a specific evaluation, and Appendix A lists all 120 evaluations by identifier with the component, package, outcome, and evidence type. Identifiers are numbered consecutively within each category, except that ContentProvider identifiers run to CP-34 although 29 are counted: three duplicate positive controls NEG-06 to NEG-08, and two require ADB access (Section 3.1 ). Figure 2 summarizes the study workflow. 1. Select component and evaluation category 2. Determine expected enforcement 3. Test observed enforcement (PoC / code review) 4. Classify outcome: GAP or HOLDS 5. Assign taxonomy category (T1–T4) 6. Record evidence type (S, D, or S+D) specification, docs, sibling comparison Figure 2: Per-evaluation workflow. Steps 2–6 are applied to each of the 120 evaluations. Expected enforcement is derived from specification, documentation, protection-level semantics, or sibling comparison. 3.4 Evaluation Scope In scope: Android phone inter-component interfaces on a Google Pixel 6a running Android 17 (API 37, builds CP2A.260605.012 and CP31.260608.007). Google and AOSP first-party applications, including Chrome and Fitbit. Out of scope: Wear OS components (separate security model), kernel/Binder-layer analysis (below the IPC abstraction), network-level attacks, and WebView/JavaScript bridge security, with one exception (SYS-10, Section 4.7 ). 3.5 Limitations of Methodology Our evaluations are not randomly sampled; the researcher selected boundaries based on judgment about where gaps might exist, biasing the gap rate upward. The 80.8% gap rate characterizes the evaluated corpus, not all Android IPC boundaries. Twenty-one evaluations (17.5%) are based on static analysis only and lack runtime confirmation. Evaluations cover a single device (Pixel 6a) and Android version (17). The study focuses on Google/AOSP first-party apps; findings may not generalize to the broader Android app ecosystem. App versions are as installed at evaluation time; Google apps receive frequent updates. 4 Results Throughout this section, identifiers in parentheses, such as (CP-06) or (A-12), point to individual evaluations; Appendix A gives the full entry for each. 4.1 Enforcement Landscape Table 2 summarizes enforcement outcomes across all evaluation categories. Of 120 evaluations, 97 (80.8%) exhibit enforcement gaps and 23 (19.2%) exhibit functioning enforcement. Within our purposively selected corpus, observed enforcement outcomes differ substantially: Activities, BroadcastReceivers, custom URI schemes, and platform controls show 100% gap rates, while ContentProviders and Services show lower gap rates (72.4% and 71.4%), that is, holds rates of 27.6% and 28.6%. The 100% rate for custom URI schemes is structural rather than a per-application failure: the platform cannot verify any custom scheme (Section 4.6 ), so every scheme selected for carrying sensitive data is a gap. OAuth/authentication callbacks (A-01–A-03). Three authentication callback Activities in Gmail and GMS accept arbitrary callers. CseRedirectUriReceiverActivity (Gmail) processes OAuth callback data from any application. BrowserSignInResponseHandlerActivity (GMS) handles Firebase Auth callbacks on both HTTPS and HTTP schemes without origin verification. AuthzenDeeplinkHandlerActivity (GMS) handles sign-in challenge links without verifying the caller. Payment Activities (A-04–A-07). Four Activities in Google Wallet and GMS handle payment-related operations without adequate caller verification. FinishAndroidAppRedirectProxyActivity forwards caller-controlled URLs through GMS’s process context. AddNewCardThroughBrowserActivity accepts card-tokenization requests from any caller. PresentationModeActivity activates NFC tap-to-pay without lock screen authentication. Wallet’s DeepLinkActivity declares android:autoVerify , but that attribute only governs implicit intents, so any application can open its deep-link routes with an explicit intent. Credential and identity Activities (A-08, A-09). SharePasswordsActivity (GMS) accepts an arbitrary requesting agent name and package in its credential-sharing flow, and a diagnostics tool’s login Activity uses an authentication check that always succeeds. Debug Activities (A-10, A-11). CalendarDebugActivity runs in the CalendarProvider process, allowing any caller to bypass the READ_CALENDAR permission check. ContactsDumpActivity zips and serves the entire contacts data directory without access control. Confused deputy (A-12–A-17). Six Activities act on a caller’s behalf with privileges the caller lacks, the confused deputy pattern [ 12 ] . Three render protected data directly: LaunchInfoActivity renders calendar events without requiring READ_CALENDAR , QuickContactActivity renders full contact cards without READ_CONTACTS , and HostPhotoPagerActivity renders photos without READ_MEDIA_IMAGES . Three relay caller-controlled requests under the target application’s identity: BetterBug’s DispatchActivity forwards intents to an Activity protected by the DUMP permission (A-15), SystemUI’s MediaProjectionPermissionActivity reads the package name for its consent-reuse check from an attacker-controlled extra when the caller is unknown (A-16, static evidence), and a Play Store Activity forwards a caller-controlled URI from the Play Store process (A-17, static evidence). DoS and inconsistent validation (A-18–A-23). Five Activities crash when they receive empty or malformed Intents, causing process-level denial of service (A-18, A-20–A-23). KeyChainActivity (A-20) crashes the system-UID process; BrightnessDialog (A-22) crashes the main SystemUI process. In the same group, a Dialer handler (A-19) is the only one of its sibling handlers that omits the Google signature check the others apply. PII exposure and privileged configuration (A-24–A-27). An emergency-information screen designed for the lock screen is exported to any application and exposes the owner’s name, medical information, and emergency contacts (A-24). Three Activities perform privileged configuration without the permission their context implies: a Wi-Fi calling activation screen whose sibling Activities require MODIFY_PHONE_STATE (A-25), an eSIM download screen that accepts a forced-provisioning flag from any caller (A-26), and a parental-controls setup Activity reachable without a manifest permission (A-27, static evidence). 4.3 ContentProvider Boundary Findings (B2) Of 29 evaluated ContentProvider boundaries, 21 exhibit gaps and 8 exhibit holds, the highest holds rate of any interface category. SQL injection (CP-01–CP-13). CalendarProvider2 accepts unsanitized input in its selection, projection, and write-path (update and delete) parameters, permitting cross-table data extraction (CP-01–CP-03), and the platform change that would enforce strict query validation for it is disabled (CP-04; see SYS-01). Selection injection also reaches ContactsProvider2, CallLogProvider, and CarrierIdProvider, the last with full UNION injection and no permission required (CP-05, CP-07, CP-08); sortOrder injection affects four providers (CP-09); and CellBroadcastContentProvider applies none of the strict-mode checks (CP-10, static evidence). Where the defenses are applied, they hold: ContactsProvider2 blocks projection injection via setStrict(true) (CP-06), CalendarProvider2’s instances query enables all three strict-mode checks (CP-11), and MediaProvider and DownloadProvider reject SQL keywords in sortOrder (CP-12, CP-13). Shared library gap (CP-14–CP-19). Four Google Workspace applications (Drive, Docs, Sheets, Slides) share a LegacyStorageBackendContentProvider with zero permission checks on query() (CP-14–CP-17). The modern StorageBackendContentProvider in the same packages correctly requires MANAGE_DOCUMENTS (CP-18, HOLDS), and the legacy provider’s openFile() resists path traversal because it looks files up by database identifier rather than building a filesystem path from the request (CP-19, HOLDS). Asymmetric permissions (CP-23, CP-24). MmsSmsProvider declares readPermission but no writePermission , allowing deletion of SMS/MMS records. GoogleSettingsProvider declares writePermission but no readPermission , exposing 18 partner settings. Other provider gaps (CP-20–CP-22, CP-25, CP-27, CP-34). A debug provider serves a ZIP archive of the contacts database (CP-20); Settings’ SuggestionStateProvider reveals screen-lock and biometric enrollment status (CP-21); Messages’ AvatarContentProvider proxies arbitrary content:// URIs under its own READ_CONTACTS permission (CP-22); ServiceStateProvider skips its permission checks for callers targeting API levels below 31 (CP-25); GServicesProvider is guarded only by a normal-level permission while exposing 1,404 configuration entries (CP-27); and a temporary URI grant from the contact picker permits SQL injection that reaches all internal ContactsProvider2 tables (CP-34). Of the identifiers CP-28 to CP-33, three duplicate positive controls (CP-28 to CP-30) and one falls outside the attacker model (CP-33, Section 3.1 ). The other two are counted holds: BluetoothOppProvider applies setStrict(true) and a path permission (CP-31), and the phone application’s SIM contact providers require contacts permissions (CP-32). 4.4 BroadcastReceiver Boundary Findings (B3) All 11 evaluated BroadcastReceiver boundaries exhibit gaps. GmsExternalReceiver (BR-01–BR-03). GMS uses a single exported receiver for 31 distinct Intent actions with no android:permission and no per-action sender validation (BR-03). Behind it, FrpUpdateIntentOperation writes the Factory Reset Protection (FRP) secret without sender verification (BR-01), and AuthZenEventHandler forces re-registration of six CryptAuth security keys (BR-02). Debug receivers (BR-04–BR-06). TestingToolsBroadcastReceiver is present in 11 Google applications, gated by a runtime Phenotype flag (Google’s server-controlled feature-flag system) rather than stripped at build time (BR-04). CalendarProvider’s debug receiver responds to a secret-code broadcast (BR-05), and a test receiver in com.google.android.apps.scone forwards simulated state changes to a privileged service (BR-06). Safety-critical receiver (BR-08). CrisisNotificationBroadcastReceiver accepts broadcast intents from any application, enabling dismissal of earthquake, tsunami, and active shooter alerts. Other receivers (BR-07, BR-09–BR-11). SystemUI’s media-output dialog action is not declared as a protected broadcast although its sibling action is (BR-07); an OMA-DM receiver without a permission invokes a permission-protected receiver directly as a Java method, bypassing the system’s broadcast permission check (BR-09); Wallet receivers let any application cancel Wallet notifications, including fraud alerts (BR-10); and the Messages RCS provisioning receiver relies on a normal-level permission and validates the sender for only one of its seven actions (BR-11). 4.5 Service Boundary Findings (B4) Of 14 evaluated Service boundaries, 10 exhibit gaps and 4 exhibit holds. MediaBrowserService pattern (SV-01, SV-02). YouTube’s MediaBrowserService only blocks SystemUI, accepting all other callers with zero permissions. Bluetooth’s MediaBrowserService accepts all callers with zero validation. Missing or weak service permissions (SV-03–SV-06, SV-09, SV-10). GMS exports 126 services without android:permission (SV-03), and Photos exports seven backup services without permission while keeping its internal backup services unexported (SV-04). Messages and the Google app guard services with normal-level permissions that every application receives automatically (SV-05, SV-10). FederatedCompute performs no Binder caller checks anywhere in its service (SV-06), and an on-device personalization service lacks the permission its sibling service requires (SV-09). Inconsistent AIDL enforcement (SV-07, SV-08). KeyChainService exposes approximately 50 Binder methods; 5 lack caller identity checks, allowing enumeration of 120 system certificate authority (CA) certificate aliases. NfcService protects all but 2 of approximately 50 methods; the two unprotected methods accept forged host card emulation (HCE) data. Positive controls (SV-11–SV-14). FelicaServiceImpl enforces getCallingUid() (SV-11). ZeroPartyBinder performs UID plus signature verification (SV-12). NfcService enforces NFC permissions on all its other methods (SV-13).
